c.tagline: France's South Pacific capital — a lively island port, colorful market and gateway to Tahiti and the Society Islands.

taxi.fareNote: There are no ride-hailing apps (no Uber or Lyft) in French Polynesia. Taxis are few, expensive and often unmetered with fixed island rates, so agree the price before getting in; most visitors rely on hotel transfers, le truck buses or a rental car instead.

emergency.note: As a French territory the European numbers apply: 15 for medical (SAMU), 17 for police and 18 for the fire service; 112 also works from any mobile.

avoid.reason: Watch for petty theft around the waterfront, market and dimly lit port-side streets after dark.

hood_desc: The bustling heart of the capital around the Marche de Papeete municipal market, the Pomare Boulevard waterfront, Notre Dame Cathedral and the roulotte food trucks of Place Vaiete; the walkable base for first-timers and cruise arrivals, liveliest by day and after dark.
A working marina and light-industrial peninsula just north of downtown, home to boatyards, the yacht quay and marine services; handy to the centre but functional rather than scenic.
The reclaimed port island holding Papeete's commercial harbour, container terminal and the inter-island ferry docks for Moorea and the outer islands; a transit hub rather than a place to stay.

A leafy, upscale residential commune immediately east of the capital, home to government offices, quiet lagoon frontage and the long-standing Hotel Royal Tahitien; calmer and greener than the city centre.

An affluent coastal suburb southwest of the capital with the best beaches near town, the Museum of Tahiti and Her Islands, lagoon resorts and sunset views toward Moorea; favored for a relaxed resort base.

water.note: Tap water in Papeete is treated and safe, but use bottled on the outer islands.

transit.pay: Fares on the RTC bus network (the buses that replaced the old open-sided le truck) are paid in cash to the driver or with a rechargeable card; a single ride is a few hundred CFP francs. There is no rail or metro of any kind.
transit.hours: Buses run mainly during daytime hours on weekdays with sparse evening and weekend service, so timetables are unreliable for tight plans; taxis and rental cars fill the gaps.
transit.note: Papeete has no rail transit. The RTC bus network covers the built-up west coast between Papeete and the outlying communes, but service is infrequent, so most visitors use hotel transfers, a rental car, or the ferries to reach Moorea and the airport.

tip.r: Tipping is not customary in French Polynesia; service is included and locals do not expect it, though rounding up for exceptional service is welcome.

landmarks: Papeete Municipal Market
The vibrant two-story marché overflowing with tropical flowers, fresh fish, vanilla, and monoi oil is the beating heart of Tahitian daily life.
Notre-Dame Cathedral of Papeete
This red-and-white 19th-century cathedral in the city center is Papeete's most recognizable religious landmark and a striking photo subject.
Papeete Waterfront (Rade de Papeete)
The palm-lined harbor promenade framed by yachts, ferries, and Moorea's silhouette across the channel makes for classic golden-hour shots.
Point Venus Lighthouse
The historic black-and-white lighthouse on the black-sand point where Captain Cook observed the transit of Venus is one of Tahiti's most photographed sites.
Arahoho Blowhole (Trou du Souffleur)
Powerful surf blasts seawater skyward through a natural lava-rock vent along the dramatic east coast road, a favorite roadside photo stop.
Papeete Town Hall (Mairie de Papeete)
A grand colonial-style building modeled on Queen Pomare's former palace, offering elegant tropical architecture in the city center.
Paofai Protestant Temple
This iconic white Protestant church near the waterfront, famous for its Tahitian choir, is a cultural cornerstone and photogenic landmark.
Faarumai Waterfalls (Les Trois Cascades)
A short jungle walk leads to three cascading waterfalls tumbling into a fern-fringed pool, one of Tahiti's most scenic natural spots.
Vaipahi Water Gardens
Lush tropical gardens with lily ponds, streams, and a hidden waterfall make this a tranquil, highly photogenic escape near Papeete.
Kanti Chinese Temple
A colorful, ornately decorated Chinese temple reflecting Tahiti's Hakka Chinese heritage adds unexpected cultural flair to Papeete.

train.note: There is no railway anywhere in French Polynesia. A short industrial tramway served the sugar and phosphate trade on Tahiti in the 19th century but nothing of it survives, and the island is circled by a single coastal road instead. All travel beyond Tahiti is by boat or plane.

bus.note: No bus route leaves French Polynesia - the nearest land is thousands of kilometres away, so every international arrival comes through Faa'a airport or the cruise quay. Around Tahiti, the Tere Tahiti network (https://www.teretahiti.pf/) runs air-conditioned buses from the terminal on the Papeete waterfront along the north and south coasts of the island and past the airport, with fares paid by contactless card or cash to the driver. Services thin out sharply after early evening and on Sundays and public holidays, so most visitors hire a car or rely on taxis for anything outside the city centre.

intl.to: Moorea (French Polynesia) - sails from the downtown ferry quay on the Papeete waterfront, carries cars
Moorea (French Polynesia) - sails from the downtown ferry quay on the Papeete waterfront
Marquesas, Tuamotu & Society Islands (French Polynesia) - mixed cargo-passenger voyages from the Motu Uta port north of the centre

ferry.note: All ferries from Papeete are domestic inter-island services; there are no international ferry routes from Tahiti. The Aremiti and Terevau fast ferries cross to Moorea in about 30-45 minutes several times a day from the downtown ferry quay, a few minutes' walk from the market, and take cars as well as foot passengers, with tickets valid for months and no need to book far ahead. Slower cargo-passenger ships for the Tuamotus, Marquesas and Australs leave from Motu Uta, among them the Aranui 5, whose 12-day Marquesas circuits carry about 230 passengers and are usually booked many months in advance. Small local schooners to nearby islands sell tickets at the quay on the day and keep loose schedules that shift with the freight.

half.name: Moorea
half.blurb: A lagoon island ringed by jagged volcanic peaks is reached by a thirty-minute ferry from Papeete.

full.name: Tetiaroa
full.blurb: Marlon Brando's former private atoll, with pristine motus and a lagoon reef, is reached by a short plane flight.
